chapter: Bunk Johnson and American Music records
title: Starting American Music: the Jazzmen records made on a toy machine
summary: Perhonas asks how American Music began, and Russell begins with the badly recorded 1942 Bunk sides that Dave Stewart issued.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Do you have any other questions there?

Well, yeah, just with, I know that you recorded Bunk Johnson's band on your own record label. And I wanted to just ask you a little bit about how the American Records Company, I think was the name of your...
Yeah, just call it American Music.
American Music got started and how that relates to Bunk Johnson being well known. Or did that help his cause? Yeah, we might talk a little about that.

The reason I got into the business at all was partly due to these first records I mentioned, the Jazzmen, that were so badly recorded on the little machine. About a $200 list price machine it was, a federal recorder. Some kid that worked, he was a teenage kid, I guess, that worked for Grunewald's. Happened to have it. He's the only one we could find that had any blanks around that would be able to record the band in 1942 when Dave issued the records. And those records were so bad that I'll tell you one story that I'll illustrate it. Dave wanted to stop, take his time. He was driving back to California, so he packed up the masters about a dozen sides or so. On steel, they were steel base, I guess. They weren't glass. He wouldn't have shipped them. They were steel base acetates. And I think it was Allied recording, the biggest factory out there. They had a studio, too, in Los Angeles. And they'd been pressing the Lou Waters records for him. So he sent these masters on to his friend, who was the engineer, somebody there, and told him to start work on them so he'd be ready to issue them, you know, when he got back or something. So he got back maybe a week or maybe almost two weeks later. And so he goes there to the studio to get the records and see what work's been done. And the guy started laughing. He said, Oh, he said, you really meant that? He thought it was a joke. He thought they sent him those things just as a horrible example, you know, of how bad recording could be. And... ... ...
